display.title: Through the Eyes of a Tzaddik, Part 2
display.summary_short: Before Shavuos, why the Torah's mitzvos are true freedom. Then Reb Baruch obeys the Alter Rebbe, goes to the minister a week late, and learns how the delay saved his life.
display.summary_long: Before continuing the story, the storyteller speaks about Shavuos. Leaving Egypt had a goal: to serve Hashem at Har Sinai. But how is trading Pharaoh's rules for 613 mitzvos called freedom? The Rebbe's parable explains: a plant, an animal and a person each need different things to feel free, and a Jewish neshamah is free only when it lives with Torah and mitzvos. A second parable tells of a wingless bird who refuses an eagle's gift of wings because they look heavy, until he learns that wings lift you up when you use them, just like mitzvos done with joy. The Rebbe once told a professor that the greatest miracle in history is that the Jewish people still exist. Then the story continues: after a week, the Alter Rebbe tells Reb Baruch he may now go to the minister and will find favor. The guards rush him in, and the overjoyed minister explains that an officer had been ordered to shoot him on sight that Tuesday, but he did not come, and the next day witnesses revealed that Ivan had framed him. Reb Baruch gets his job back with a raise and understands that everything looks different through the eyes of a tzaddik.
display.lesson: Torah and mitzvos are true freedom that lift us up, and following a tzaddik's guidance with trust in Hashem brings protection.

advisories.note: The minister reveals an officer had orders to shoot Reb Baruch on sight; he was never in danger in the end.
A Jew-hater frames a Chassid; the survival of the Jewish people after persecutions is mentioned.
